parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A man books a room at a conference centre for a workshop.
script: Good morning, Quayside Conference Centre, Sophie speaking.
Hello. I'd like to book a room for a one-day workshop.
Certainly. Could I have your name?
Dr Ravi Menon. M, E, N, O, N.
And which organisation is the booking for?
What date are you looking at?
And how many people are you expecting?
Our Garden Room only holds thirty, so I'd suggest the Harbour Room, which can take up to sixty.
How would you like the seating arranged? In rows, or in groups at round tables?
In groups, please. There'll be a lot of discussion.
And what equipment will you need?
A projector, of course, and a microphone, because some of our speakers are quite softly spoken.
No problem. For lunch, we offer either a sandwich lunch or a hot buffet.
The hot buffet, please. It's quite a long day.
The total for the room, refreshments and the hot buffet comes to forty-two pounds per person.
We'll need final numbers by the tenth of October, one week before the event.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A farm manager speaks to teachers about visiting a city farm.
script: Hello everyone, and thanks for coming. I'm Dave, the manager here at Millbrook City Farm, and I'd like to tell you what your classes can expect when they visit.
The farm was set up in 1985 on land that used to be a railway yard. When the trains stopped, local residents campaigned to turn it into a green space instead of a car park.
Our main aim is to show city children where their food comes from. Many of the children who visit have never seen a cow or a vegetable growing in the ground.
There's one rule we're very strict about. After touching any animal, children must wash their hands at the sinks by the entrance. It's very important for hygiene.
Our shop sells eggs from our own hens, as well as honey from a local beekeeper. Teachers often buy a box of eggs for the class.
Now, the different areas. In the goat shed, children can watch the goats being milked in the morning.
In the hen house, they can help to collect the eggs. They usually love that.
At the vegetable plots, each group can plant some seeds to take back to school.
At the pond, we do pond-dipping with nets, looking for frogs, snails and insects.
The pig pen is where children can feed the animals, using special food that we provide.
And in the pony paddock, younger children can have short rides, at weekends only.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two students, Fatima and Ethan, discuss their survey about how students travel to campus.
script: Fatima, let's look at the results of our travel survey before we write the proposal.
Sure. Remember, the reason we did it was that the university plans to reduce the number of car parking spaces next year.
Right. And we got four hundred responses, which is far more than we expected.
The posters with QR codes worked much better than I thought. Hardly anyone responded to the emails.
What surprised you most in the results?
That about a third of the students who drive live less than three kilometres from campus.
That's a short distance. So what's our main proposal?
I think discounted bus passes. It would encourage people to leave their cars at home.
Agreed. And we're presenting it to the student union committee next month.
Yes. Let's go through the main complaints about each type of transport. For the bus, it was mainly that buses are unreliable and often late.
For the train, the problem was cost. Tickets are expensive, even with a student railcard.
Cyclists said there's nowhere secure to leave their bikes on campus.
And people who walk complained about safety, especially the paths with no lighting in winter.
Their main complaint was the time it takes to find a parking space in the mornings.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecture on fungi and their uses.
script: Today we're going to look at fungi, a group of organisms that are often overlooked but are essential to life on Earth.
Fungi were once classified as plants, but they're actually more closely related to animals. Unlike plants, they can't make their own food from sunlight. They feed by breaking down other material.
What we see as a mushroom is only a small part of a fungus. The main body is underground: a network called mycelium, made up of tiny threads called hyphae.
Some fungi grow to enormous sizes. A honey fungus in Oregon, in the United States, covers around nine square kilometres, making it one of the largest living organisms ever found.
Fungi are hugely important to medicine. Many antibiotics, which have saved millions of lives, are produced by fungi.

Today, scientists and companies are finding new uses. Mycelium can be grown into moulds to make packaging, replacing polystyrene, which is very difficult to recycle. It can also be processed into a material that looks and feels like leather.
Researchers have even made building bricks from mycelium. They can be grown in about five days, using agricultural waste, and they're light and fireproof.
Some fungi can break down pollutants, and they've been tested as a way of cleaning up oil spills.
Fungi can also cause serious problems. A fungal disease called Panama disease is currently threatening banana crops around the world.
Finally, there is still a great deal we don't know. Scientists estimate that there may be several million species of fungi, but fewer than ten percent have been described.

passages.title: A Cold History
paragraphs: Long before refrigerators, people found ways to enjoy frozen treats. In ancient Persia, engineers built yakhchal, large dome-shaped ice houses with thick walls, in which ice collected in winter could be stored through the hot desert summer. The ice was used to chill drinks and make sweet frozen desserts. In China during the Tang dynasty, there are records of a frozen dish made from milk.

A popular story claims that the Venetian traveller Marco Polo brought recipes for ice cream from China to Italy in the thirteenth century. There is, however, no evidence to support this, and most historians regard it as a myth.

A key scientific discovery made modern ice cream possible. When salt is added to ice, it lowers the temperature at which the ice melts, producing a mixture much colder than ice alone. This effect was known in the Arab world by the thirteenth century, and it allowed cooks to freeze mixtures of cream and sugar placed in a container surrounded by salted ice.

By the seventeenth century, frozen desserts were fashionable in Europe. In Naples, the cook Antonio Latini published recipes for sorbets, including one made with milk, in the 1690s. In Paris, the Café Procope, which opened in 1686, became famous for serving ices to its customers, and it helped to make them popular among the wider public.

Ice cream reached America with European settlers and quickly became popular among the wealthy. Records show that George Washington spent around 200 dollars on ice cream during a single summer in 1790, a very large sum at the time. It became more widely available after 1843, when Nancy Johnson of Philadelphia patented a hand-cranked freezer that made the process much easier. She sold the patent for 200 dollars.

The ice cream cone became popular at the World's Fair held in St Louis in 1904, although similar edible cones had existed earlier. Today, ice cream is a global industry, and it is eaten in enormous quantities: in countries such as New Zealand, Australia and the United States, the average person consumes many litres every year.

passages.title: Racing the Wave
paragraphs: On 26 December 2004, a massive earthquake off the coast of Sumatra in Indonesia triggered a series of tsunamis that swept across the Indian Ocean. Waves struck coastlines in more than a dozen countries, from Thailand to Somalia, killing around 230,000 people. Many of the deaths occurred hours after the earthquake, in places far from its centre. Yet, unlike the Pacific, the Indian Ocean had no system to warn people that a tsunami was coming.

Most tsunamis are caused by earthquakes beneath the sea floor, which suddenly lift or drop a section of the seabed and displace a huge volume of water. In the deep ocean, a tsunami can travel at up to 800 kilometres per hour, as fast as a jet aircraft, yet its height may be less than a metre, so ships may not even notice it passing. Only as it approaches shallow water near the coast does it slow down and grow into a towering wall of water.

Detecting tsunamis in the open ocean requires special equipment. The most important tools are DART buoys, which combine a pressure sensor on the seabed with a buoy on the surface. When a tsunami passes, the weight of water above the sensor changes slightly, and the change is sent by satellite to warning centres. After 2004, a network of such buoys was installed in the Indian Ocean, and a regional warning system began operating in 2011.

Detecting a tsunami is only half of the challenge. Warnings must also reach people on the coast in time, which experts call the 'last-mile' problem. Messages from national warning centres have to be passed on to local communities through sirens, radio, text messages and loudspeakers in mosques and temples, and people must know what to do when they hear them. In remote areas, this can be the weakest part of the system.

Sometimes, knowledge saves lives where technology does not. In 2004, a ten-year-old British girl, Tilly Smith, was on holiday in Thailand when she noticed the sea suddenly drawing back from the beach. She remembered a geography lesson about tsunamis and warned her parents, who helped clear the beach, saving around a hundred people. On the Indonesian island of Simeulue, very close to the earthquake, only a handful of people died, because an oral tradition passed down since a tsunami in 1907 taught islanders to run to the hills when the ground shook.

Even the best-prepared countries can be overwhelmed. Japan has one of the most advanced warning systems in the world, but in 2011 the initial warnings underestimated the height of the tsunami, and waves overtopped many sea walls, killing more than 18,000 people. Since then, Japan has changed how it issues warnings for very large earthquakes, giving clearer instructions to evacuate immediately rather than precise wave heights.

passages.title: The Myth of Learning Styles
paragraphs: Ask a group of teachers whether students learn better when they are taught in their preferred 'learning style', and most will say yes. Surveys in several countries have found that around nine out of ten teachers believe in the idea. The most popular version, known as VAK, divides learners into three types: visual learners, who learn best from pictures and diagrams; auditory learners, who learn best by listening; and kinaesthetic learners, who learn best through movement and hands-on activity.

It is true that people have preferences about how they like to receive information. Some enjoy diagrams, others prefer to listen to explanations. The question is whether matching teaching to these preferences actually improves learning. This idea, which researchers call the 'meshing hypothesis', is the crucial claim on which the whole theory depends.

In 2008, a team of psychologists led by Harold Pashler reviewed the research. They pointed out that a proper test would require dividing students according to their style, teaching each group in different ways, and showing that each group did best when the teaching matched its style. They found almost no studies that met this standard, and those that did generally failed to support the theory. They concluded that there was no adequate evidence to justify using learning styles in education.

Later studies have reached similar conclusions. In one experiment, Beth Rogowsky and her colleagues tested adults who said they preferred learning either by reading or by listening, and gave them a text either in written form or as an audiobook. Matching the format to their preference made no difference to how well they understood it.

What does seem to matter is the nature of the content. A lesson on geography is best taught with maps, whatever a student's supposed style, and learning to play the piano requires practice with the hands. There is also good evidence for what psychologists call dual coding: presenting information in both words and pictures tends to help all learners, not just those labelled 'visual'.

In my view, the persistence of the learning styles myth is not harmless. Many schools have spent time and money testing students to identify their style, and some children have been told that they are 'kinaesthetic learners' who cannot learn well from reading, a label that may limit what they attempt. I believe teachers would serve their students better by using methods that research has shown to work, such as regular testing, spacing practice over time and combining words with images.

task1.text: The bar chart below shows average rainfall, in millimetres, in selected months in Dhaka and London. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
model: The bar chart compares the average rainfall in Dhaka and London in six months of the year: January, March, May, July, September and November.

Overall, the two cities have very different patterns. Rainfall in Dhaka varies dramatically, with very wet months in the middle of the year and very dry months at the beginning and end. In London, by contrast, rainfall is moderate and fairly constant throughout the year.

In Dhaka, January is extremely dry, with only 7 mm of rain on average, and the figure for March is also low, at 60 mm. Rainfall then increases sharply to 300 mm in May and reaches a peak of 400 mm in July, before falling slightly to 320 mm in September. By November, it has dropped to just 30 mm.

London's rainfall stays between 40 and 60 mm in all six months, with November the wettest at 60 mm and March the driest at 40 mm. As a result, London receives more rain than Dhaka in January and November, but in July Dhaka receives almost nine times as much as London.

task2.text: Some people believe that governments should put a tax on sugary foods and drinks to improve public health. To what extent do you agree or disagree? Write at least 250 words.
model: Rates of obesity and type 2 diabetes have risen sharply in many countries, and sugar is widely seen as one of the main causes. As a result, several governments have introduced taxes on sugary drinks and foods. I largely agree with this policy, although I believe it should be part of a wider strategy rather than a solution on its own.

The main argument in favour of a sugar tax is that price influences behaviour. When sugary drinks become more expensive, people tend to buy fewer of them, particularly young people and those on low incomes, who are often most affected by diet-related illness. A tax can also encourage manufacturers to reduce the amount of sugar in their products. After the United Kingdom introduced a levy on soft drinks in 2018, many companies reformulated their drinks to avoid the tax, significantly reducing the sugar people consumed. In addition, the money raised can be spent on health programmes, such as sport in schools.

Critics argue that such taxes are unfair, because they take a larger share of income from poorer households, and that adults should be free to make their own choices about what they eat. They also point out that sugar is only one part of an unhealthy diet, and that taxing it alone will not solve obesity.

These criticisms have some validity, but they are not convincing reasons to reject the tax. The health benefits are likely to be greatest for poorer families, and revenue can be used to support them. However, the tax must be combined with other measures, such as clearer food labelling, restrictions on advertising to children and better education about nutrition.
In conclusion, I agree that a tax on sugary products is a useful tool for improving public health, provided that it forms part of a broader approach.

speaking.cue:
Describe an interesting conversation you had with someone you didn't know well.
You should say:
- who the person was
- where you had the conversation
- what you talked about
and explain why it was interesting.
speaking.cueModel: I'd like to describe a conversation I had with an elderly man on a long-distance bus from Dhaka to Chittagong last year. I was sitting by the window reading, and he was in the seat next to me. At first we didn't speak, but when the bus stopped for a break, he asked me what I was studying. When I told him computer science, he got very excited, because it turned out he'd been an engineer at the national telephone company in the nineteen-seventies. For the next three hours, he told me stories about how phone lines were installed in rural areas, how people used to book calls days in advance, and how the whole village would gather when someone received a call from abroad. I told him about my studies and the kind of apps students build now, and he kept shaking his head in amazement. What made the conversation so interesting was that it made me see technology from a completely different perspective. I take instant communication for granted, but for him it was something almost magical. It also reminded me that people who seem quiet and ordinary often have fascinating stories, if you just take the time to ask.
